1:
The command to ask is continuous with what went before. Clarke says the promise of plenty at the close of the last chapter leads the prophet to name the means of obtaining it, supplication to the Lord and not to idols, whose worship had proved a fertile source of calamities. Henry makes it a principle: gracious things having been promised, God intimates that he will for these things be enquired of, and expects to be acknowledged rather than the idols that rivalled him. They are not to pray to the clouds nor to the stars for rain but to the Lord, since it is he that hears the heavens when they hear the earth.

Whether the summons is meant seriously is expressly raised. Keil and Delitzsch says it is not a mere turn of address expressing God's readiness to give, as one interpreter held, but is seriously meant, as the reason assigned in the next verse shows; the church is to ask of God what it needs and not trust in idols. Calvin agrees, and adds a sharper edge. One who merely reads the words may think a new subject is introduced; but the context shows the people are here condemned, since it depended on them only that they did not enjoy abundance, and the exhortation carries an implied reproof. They had closed the door against God's favour, being straitened in themselves as all the unbelieving are who cannot embrace the promises; and when the Lord withdrew his hand and they laboured under want, many made great complaints.

The two rains are described from experience. Gill places the former in autumn about seed time and the latter in spring before harvest, notes that an ancient poet calls them the autumnal and vernal rains, and that between the two there was seldom more; he cites one of the fathers, who said he had never seen rain in those countries in July. Henry gives the same two seasons and says that if either failed it went hard with the land. Clarke divides them by office, one to impregnate the seed and the other to fill the ear, so essential that the promise of rain stands among the chief of God's mercies. On the next word Ellicott prefers lightnings to bright clouds, as what precedes the longed-for rain; Keil and Delitzsch renders it the same way, and Wesley reconciles them by saying the clouds are bright through the lightnings that break from them.

Whether the idolatry reproved is present or past is the question of the second verse. Clarke says it is spoken of the people and must refer to their idolatry before the captivity, since there were no idols after it; some take the idols and diviners for those of a later Greek dynasty, and others think a captivity is being foretold, a determined future event being often spoken of as past. Ellicott meets the same point as an objection to the date of the passage, that idols and false prophets suit only a time before the exile. He grants that after the captivity idolatry was not the sin they were especially inclined to, but answers that marriage with heathen women, so often spoken of afterwards, was a continual danger, and that idolatry and soothsaying were in fact practised down to the destruction of the city, since we read of false prophets who opposed the governor and of sorcerers named by a later prophet. Gill notes that the word is teraphim, that one paraphrase understands it of the worshippers rather than the images, and that a Jewish expositor takes them for images which speak by sorceries, thought to be so formed as to talk with men. Wesley reads the consequences plainly: the predictions were vain, the going away was into captivity, and the want of a shepherd is the want of governors, civil or ecclesiastical, who would do their duty.
3:
Who the shepherds and goats are divides them first. Gill reports a paraphrase making the shepherds kings and the goats princes, and Jewish expositors who take them for foreign kings; ecclesiastical rulers may also be meant, answering to the shepherds of Israel reproved by the older prophets for ignorance, covetousness and cruelty toward the flock. Clarke identifies them as bad kings and bad priests, the goats wicked priests, shepherds by office and goats by the impurity of their lives. Wesley makes them officers in church and state, the goats like he-goats that push and trample the feebler cattle. Ellicott takes the other view: the term is used of native rulers and foreign oppressors alike, the goats are probably the shepherds themselves, and both are foreign, since the rest of the verse seems to say the whole people is to be changed from a timid flock into a nation of warriors. He also corrects two tenses, preferring is kindled and I will punish.

Out of whom the four things come is expressly disputed. Ellicott says it is much debated whether the pronoun means the Lord of hosts or the nation, and thinks it best taken of the nation; he prefers shall proceed to came forth. Wesley takes it of God, Clarke of the tribe itself, whence all strength and counsel came, and Gill of the Messiah, who was to come out of that tribe.

The figures are read closely. Ellicott takes the corner for a chieftain on whom the national fabric is put together, and the nail for a chieftain too, as him on whom everything hangs, though the figure may be the tent-peg holding the ropes; the last word he takes either as a ruler who keeps people to their work, or as an oppressor of the heathen, set against the heathen oppressor of the chapter before. Clarke reads the corner-stone as the ornament and completion of the building, the nail as that by which tents were fastened and armour hung, the bow as the choicest archers, and the oppressors as the generals by whom their foes should be routed, suggesting that perhaps the whole is spoken of the Messiah. Wesley reads the corner as the prince, the nail as what fastens the tents of war, the bow as warlike provision, and the last word as a collector of tribute, drawing the moral that it was from God a conqueror once oppressed them, and from God that they now grow strong enough to impose tribute in their turn.

Whether the strength promised is historical or spiritual divides them. Clarke identifies the mighty men with a family of deliverers and their successors, and the riders with the power that opposed them, which had much cavalry where the people had none, and was yet overcome. Gill takes them for converted Jews strong in faith and in the grace of the Messiah, whose strength is made perfect in their weakness. Henry goes further, saying the promises look beyond that people to the gospel church and all true believers. He makes the foundation of them all the clause that the Lord is with them: he espouses their cause, and if he be for them who can be against them. All their dignity and joy are owing purely to mercy, and mercy, as it supposes misery, so it excludes merit; they had been justly cast off, yet it is promised they shall be as though he had not cast them off, the transgressions for which they were rejected not only not visited but not so much as remembered, so that God will be as perfectly reconciled as if he had never contended, and the falling out of these lovers shall be the renewing rather than the weakening of love. Keil and Delitzsch keeps to the battlefield, rendering the clause of heroes treading street-mire, and says that thus equipped the people will annihilate their foes.
6:
Whether these verses look to a distant ingathering is raised at once: Clarke doubts whether they are not to be understood of the future gathering of the people in gospel times. Henry says the promises look to that people and even to the latter days of the church: preaching the gospel is God's call for souls to come to Christ, and those whom Christ redeemed by his blood God will gather by his grace; difficulties shall be got over as easily as in the older deliverance, and God himself will be their strength and their song. He adds that if God strengthens us we must bestir ourselves in the duties of the Christian life. Gill keeps to the plain sense, that the strengthening is internal and external both. Keil and Delitzsch marks the structure, that the deliverance of the northern house is described more minutely in the verses following, to remove all doubt as to the realization of the promise.

Of the second house little is said. Gill takes it of what remain of the ten tribes; Clarke notes that the tribe named was always distinguished for its valour; Wesley reads the clause about the children as a promise that the blessings shall continue through their generations.

The call that gathers them is described in two registers. Gill says the word signifies the motion of the lips with the voice and is a sign of calling, which one paraphrase renders simply that God will call for them; he takes it of the call of the gospel, the voice of Christ, soft and melodious, a sound of grace and life. The allusion is to a shepherd gathering his sheep with his pipe, which was a reed, denoting the weakness of the instrument, the ministry of the word in itself, nevertheless made the power of God unto salvation. Clarke takes the same verb the opposite way, that God will shriek for them, calling with a voice so shrill and strong that they shall know it for the voice of their redemption. Wesley stands between: though scattered far off he will call them as a shepherd, and they shall run back to the flock. Keil and Delitzsch renders it that he will hiss to them and gather them, since he has redeemed them, and they will multiply as they have multiplied.

Ellicott turns the verse into an argument about the date of these chapters. Some critics, he says, have thought the promise of a further redemption conclusive against a post-exilic origin; but an earlier chapter speaks in similar terms of bringing the people to dwell in the city, and its genuineness has never been questioned. The fact is that the first restoration was most incomplete, only some forty-two thousand returning under the governor who led it, with a further return some twenty years after the probable date of these prophecies. On the perfect tense he notes that the decree had gone forth and been in part executed already.

The last figure is guarded against a misreading. Ellicott says the verb rendered sow is never used in the bad sense of scattering but means to spread and multiply, so there is no word of a new dispersion here but of an in-gathering; they turn again, he adds, because they remember God in the land of their captivity. Wesley reads it the same way, their increase being like that of rich soil with much seed cast upon it. Gill takes the sowing among the Gentile world as the conversion of that nation, who will become the good seed that hears the word and brings forth fruit, planted in gospel churches where the word is truly preached. Clarke reads it as reach rather than increase: wherever they have been dispersed the voice of God in the preaching of the gospel shall reach them, and they and their children shall turn again through their King.
10:
The gathering is described as a general one. Clarke says God will bring them out of all the countries where they have been dispersed and back to their own land, so numerous that they shall scarcely find in all its length and breadth a sufficiency of room; if all who are now scattered over the earth were gathered together they would make a mighty nation. He turns it into an argument from providence: as a wonderful providence has preserved them in every place, so a wondrous providence will collect them from every place of their dispersion, and when the great call comes no one soul of them shall be left behind. Gill notes only that one old paraphrase renders the clause otherwise.

Who passes through the sea is the hardest question here, and Gill lays out four answers without settling on one. It may be the people themselves, as when they came out of the land to which the allusion is made. It may be the wind, as one Jewish expositor supplies the subject, so that the sea shall become dry, being in fact a river. It may be affliction itself, as many supply it, passing through the sea in the sense of the nations, which are many as the sea, as another expositor interprets the figure. Or the words may denote the sea of this world and the afflictions of it, which the Lord causes his people to pass through and out of. Ellicott settles the subject at once, that it is God, and turns instead to the second half of the phrase, preferring the sea where affliction or straitness is to the sea with affliction, unless with one scholar the reading is taken as the sea of affliction.

What the sea itself stands for is answered from the history. Clarke hears an allusion both to the passage of the Red Sea at the coming out of one land and to the crossing of the river at the entry into the other, the waters of both thrown from side to side until all had passed safely through; and he draws the inference, that when they return God will work, if necessary, miracles like those he worked for their forefathers, so that the people among whom they live shall be glad to let them go, however much they may be profited by having them. Wesley reads the whole verse the same way, as an allusion to the two famous deliverances, with the destruction of the one power and deliverance from the bondage of the other. Both take the closing clauses literally, that the powers which oppose, as those two did formerly, shall be brought down and their sceptre broken.

The last verse turns on who is meant by the Lord in whom they are strengthened. Clarke takes the speaker to be the God of Israel and the one in whom they are strengthened to be the Messiah, supporting it from a paraphrase which reads that they shall be strengthened by the Word of the Lord, the same personal Word so often met with in those paraphrases; on this reading God speaks not of himself but concerning his Christ, and the walking up and down is in the name of the Messiah. He carries the promise further than the nation: they shall have complete liberty and appear everywhere as part of the flock of Christ, no difference made between them and the converted Gentiles, all one fold under one Shepherd. Gill is content to fix the persons, that those strengthened are not the two nations just named but the people of God. Wesley reads the walking up and down as the managing of all their affairs, and the name as the power and wisdom given from above, to the glory of God and of their Redeemer.
